Obtain sputum or another appropriate specimen for a WHO-recommended rapid molecular test (for example Xpert MTB/RIF or Ultra), microscopy and culture/drug-susceptibility testing as indicated by national guidance.

snip.t: The diagnosis of *T. vaginalis* relies on microscopy, culture, antigen detection, and molecular tests, with NAAT being the most sensitive.

qs.q: A molecular test detects rifampicin resistance. What is the next step?
o: Urgent DR-TB programme linkage and further resistance testing
Assumption of susceptibility to all other standard drugs
Addition of a single drug to the failing treatment regimen
Cessation of all treatment while waiting for resolution
qs.e: RR-TB requires prompt specialist assessment, additional susceptibility testing and an effective regimen; never add a single drug to a failing regimen.
qs.s: Tuberculosis: Advanced Clinical & Pharmacology Assessment (50 MCQs)

qs.q: A child has persistent symptoms but the initial molecular test is negative. What is the best approach?
o: Reassess clinical probability and perform additional relevant diagnostic investigations.
Exclude tuberculosis definitively based solely on the initial negative test result.
Diagnose latent tuberculosis infection relying exclusively on the presenting symptoms.
Repeat the identical molecular test continuously without further clinical evaluation.
qs.e: A negative molecular result does not fully exclude paucibacillary childhood TB. Integrate exposure, examination, imaging and further microbiology.
qs.s: Tuberculosis: Advanced Clinical & Pharmacology Assessment (50 MCQs)

qs.q: A 30-year-old pregnant woman undergoes amniocentesis. The molecular test detects a trinucleotide repeat expansion in the FMR1 gene. What is the classic clinical consequence of this mutation?
o: Spinocerebellar ataxia causing severe cerebellar and brainstem atrophy
Myotonic dystrophy featuring progressive muscle wasting and myotonia
Huntington disease presenting with involuntary choreiform movements
Friedreich ataxia marked by progressive gait ataxia and cardiomyopathy
Fragile X syndrome characterized by intellectual disability and macroorchidism
qs.e: FMR1 trinucleotide repeat expansions lead to hypermethylation and fragile X syndrome, a common cause of ID.
